description: 45 architecture firm logos explained by a brand designer, from Gensler, SOM, and Zaha Hadid Architects to BIG, Snøhetta, Foster + Partners, and Studio Gang.
intro:
Architecture firm logos have a hard job: they sign off on drawings, competition boards, and site hoardings, and they sit next to buildings that are far more spectacular than any logo. The best ones are quiet, precise, and built from type, with one idea that reflects how the studio thinks.

What makes a good architecture firm logo?

Typography first: most architecture firms use wordmarks or initials rather than symbols, like SOM, KPF, OMA, and Arup. The type itself carries the character.

One architectural idea: the best logos borrow a single idea from the work, like the cut strokes of ZHA, the shapes that spell BIG, or the line letters of Kengo Kuma & Associates.

Restraint: an architecture logo has to frame the buildings, not compete with them, so most firms stick to black, white, or one colour.

Below are 45 architecture firm logos in five groups, from the largest global firms and signature studios to international practices, design-led studios, and interior and landscape firms. Each one has a slide with my handwritten notes, followed by a short explanation. For related reading, see my guides to wordmark logos, lettermark logos, and construction logos.

logoResearch.name: Gensler
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Gensler is the largest architecture firm in the world by revenue, founded in San Francisco in 1965 by Art Gensler.
observations: A bold red wordmark in a rounded sans makes the founder's name feel friendly rather than corporate.
There is no symbol at all; the colour does the work a mark would do.

logoResearch.name: SOM
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill was founded in Chicago in 1936 and designed the Burj Khalifa.
observations: Three hairline initials replace the long partner names, like a monogram drawn with a technical pen.
The perfectly round O gives the thin letters a geometric anchor.

logoResearch.name: HOK
logoResearch.verifiedFact: HOK was founded in St. Louis in 1955 by George Hellmuth, Gyo Obata, and George Kassabaum.
observations: The initials are stacked inside a red square, so the logo reads as a stamp or a building block.
A small plus sign joins the h and k, a nod to partnership.

logoResearch.name: Perkins Eastman
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Perkins Eastman is a global architecture and planning practice founded in New York in 1981.
observations: The two names are stacked and offset, with a long rule after PERKINS that squares off the block.
Heavy capitals feel like signage on a construction site.

logoResearch.name: Perkins&Will
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Perkins&Will was founded in Chicago in 1935 and works on schools, hospitals, and offices worldwide.
observations: The ampersand pulls the two partner names into one solid word with no spaces.
A bold sans makes a 90-year-old firm look current.

logoResearch.name: HDR
logoResearch.verifiedFact: HDR is an architecture and engineering firm founded in Omaha in 1917.
observations: The H and D share a stroke, so three letters read almost like a single drawn shape.
Grey instead of black keeps the heavy letters calm.

logoResearch.name: AECOM
logoResearch.verifiedFact: AECOM is a Los Angeles-based infrastructure consulting firm working in more than 150 countries.
observations: The E is just three bars with no spine, the one quirk in a very heavy wordmark.
Black, italic-free, and wide, it is built to sit on site hoardings.

logoResearch.name: Stantec
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Stantec is a Canadian design and engineering firm founded in Edmonton in 1954.
observations: A circle with an S-shaped swoosh gives the company a symbol that works as an app icon.
The grey rounded wordmark is soft and approachable.

logoResearch.name: Arup
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Arup was founded in London in 1946 by engineer Ove Arup and engineered the Sydney Opera House.
observations: Classic serif capitals feel more like a book cover than an engineering company.
The founder's surname is short enough to need nothing else.

logoResearch.name: Zaha Hadid Architects
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Zaha Hadid Architects was founded in London in 1980 by Zaha Hadid, the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize.
observations: The letters ZHA are cut into angled pieces, echoing the sharp, fluid forms of her buildings.
Initials keep a long name compact on drawings and site boards.

logoResearch.name: BIG
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bjarke Ingels Group was founded in Copenhagen in 2005 and now also works from New York, London, and Barcelona.
observations: Three abstract shapes on a baseline spell B I G, like a section drawing of three buildings.
Read as letters or as architecture, it rewards a second look.

logoResearch.name: Foster + Partners
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Foster + Partners was founded in London in 1967 by Norman Foster and designed the Gherkin and Apple Park.
observations: A plus sign replaces the ampersand, a small engineering-like detail.
Bold, plain type mirrors the firm's clean high-tech buildings.

logoResearch.name: OMA
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Office for Metropolitan Architecture was founded in 1975 by Rem Koolhaas and partners and is based in Rotterdam.
observations: Three heavy letters set very tight form a single dense block.
The round O and A make the block feel solid, not aggressive.

logoResearch.name: Herzog & de Meuron
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Herzog & de Meuron was founded in Basel in 1978 by Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron and designed Tate Modern.
observations: The ampersand and the lowercase d keep the founders' initials honest to their real names.
Heavy type in a short abbreviation is easy to spot on a busy page.

logoResearch.name: Renzo Piano Building Workshop
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Renzo Piano Building Workshop has offices in Genoa, Paris, and New York and designed the Shard and the Centre Pompidou.
observations: Four serif capitals stand for a long name that calls the studio a workshop, not a firm.
Heavy serifs give the initials a crafted, almost carved feel.

logoResearch.name: Snøhetta
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Snøhetta was founded in Oslo in 1989 and is named after a Norwegian mountain.
observations: A small hand-drawn mountain sits after the name, literally drawing what the word means.
The Norwegian ø stays in the wordmark, keeping the local identity.

logoResearch.name: MVRDV
logoResearch.verifiedFact: MVRDV was founded in Rotterdam in 1993 and is named after its founders Winy Maas, Jacob van Rijs, and Nathalie de Vries.
observations: Condensed heavy capitals turn five initials into a tall, compact block.
The name is a code made from initials, so the type has to be strong.

logoResearch.name: Heatherwick Studio
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Heatherwick Studio was founded in London in 1994 by Thomas Heatherwick and designed Vessel and Coal Drops Yard.
observations: A classic serif makes the studio feel like a maker's workshop, not a corporation.
Studio is written in lowercase, so the founder's name leads.

logoResearch.name: Nihon Sekkei
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Nihon Sekkei is one of Japan's largest architecture and engineering firms, founded in Tokyo in 1967.
observations: A red N built from diagonal stripes gives the firm a symbol that reads at any size.
Widely spaced capitals feel calm and precise next to the bold mark.

logoResearch.name: P&T Group
logoResearch.verifiedFact: P&T Group started as Palmer & Turner in Hong Kong in 1868 and is one of Asia's oldest architecture firms.
observations: A red block with the letters PT cut into it works like a seal or a chop.
The thin GROUP under the bold P&T sets a clear order.

logoResearch.name: Sweco
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sweco is a Swedish engineering and architecture consultancy based in Stockholm.
observations: A small figure standing inside a house shape puts people at the centre of the brand.
Wide, heavy capitals keep the name sturdy.

logoResearch.name: Nikken Sekkei
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Nikken Sekkei traces its roots to 1900 in Osaka and designed the Tokyo Skytree.
observations: Thin, widely spaced capitals give the name a light, engineered feel.
A small tagline underneath explains what the firm stands for.

logoResearch.name: Kengo Kuma & Associates
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kengo Kuma & Associates was founded in Tokyo in 1990 and designed the Japan National Stadium for the Tokyo Olympics.
observations: The letters K K A A are drawn with thin lines, like timber slats in his buildings.
The logo is almost an architectural sketch rather than type.

logoResearch.name: Henning Larsen
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Henning Larsen was founded in Copenhagen in 1959 and designed the Harpa concert hall in Reykjavík.
observations: The name is stacked and offset, with a long dash closing the second line.
Bold, plain type gives a Scandinavian firm a confident voice.

logoResearch.name: Woods Bagot
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Woods Bagot was founded in Adelaide in 1869 and is now a global studio.
observations: Wide, heavy capitals stretch two surnames into one strong line.
Black and plain, the logo works on any project board.

logoResearch.name: Populous
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Populous is a Kansas City-based firm known for stadiums such as Wembley and Yankee Stadium.
observations: Wide geometric capitals with round O's echo the shape of a stadium bowl.
The name itself means crowded, a smart fit for venue design.

logoResearch.name: Hassell
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hassell was founded in Adelaide in 1938 and works across architecture, landscape, and interiors.
observations: A heavy condensed wordmark makes a short name feel tall and bold.
The double l at the end acts like two columns.

logoResearch.name: Studio Gang
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Studio Gang was founded in Chicago in 1997 by Jeanne Gang and designed the Aqua Tower.
observations: A rounded sans in deep navy feels approachable and modern.
The founder's surname reads as a word, which makes the name memorable.

logoResearch.name: KPF
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kohn Pedersen Fox was founded in New York in 1976 and designed Hudson Yards towers and the Shanghai World Financial Center.
observations: Heavy serif initials feel like the lettering on a cornerstone.
Three tight letters give a long name a strong shorthand.

logoResearch.name: Pelli Clarke & Partners
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pelli Clarke & Partners was founded in 1977 by César Pelli and designed the Petronas Towers.
observations: A light serif and a grey ampersand make the partner names elegant.
The full names stay in the logo, which feels personal.

logoResearch.name: Diller Scofidio + Renfro
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Diller Scofidio + Renfro is a New York studio that designed the High Line and The Shed.
observations: A monospaced typeface makes the names look typed, like a draft or a label.
A plus sign joins the third partner, a quirky way to show growth.

logoResearch.name: SHoP Architects
logoResearch.verifiedFact: SHoP Architects was founded in New York in 1996 and designed 111 West 57th Street.
observations: The letters interlock, with the h and p hugging the o.
A heavy lowercase gives the studio a playful voice.

logoResearch.name: Olson Kundig
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Olson Kundig is a Seattle studio founded in 1966, known for homes built from steel, glass, and timber.
observations: A light sans spells out both partner names in full.
No symbol, so the restraint mirrors the firm's quiet buildings.

logoResearch.name: Grimshaw
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Grimshaw was founded in London in 1980 by Nicholas Grimshaw and designed the Eden Project.
observations: Wide grey capitals feel solid and industrial.
The founder's name alone is enough.

logoResearch.name: Ennead
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ennead is a New York firm that grew out of Polshek Partnership and took its new name in 2010.
observations: A heavy rounded lowercase wordmark is unusual for an architecture firm.
A small line underneath explains the firm's new parent company.

logoResearch.name: Handel Architects
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Handel Architects was founded in New York in 1994 and designed the 9/11 Memorial with Michael Arad.
observations: Thin, widely spaced capitals make the name feel quiet and precise.
A tiny LLP at the end shows the firm's legal structure.

logoResearch.name: Rockwell Group
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rockwell Group was founded in New York in 1984 by David Rockwell and designs hotels, restaurants, and theatre sets.
observations: The name and the word group run together as one lowercase word.
Bold, rounded letters feel welcoming, like hospitality.

logoResearch.name: Yabu Pushelberg
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Yabu Pushelberg was founded in Toronto in 1980 by George Yabu and Glenn Pushelberg and designs luxury hotels and stores.
observations: A light, rounded lowercase gives the names a soft, refined tone.
Both founders are named, so the logo feels personal.

logoResearch.name: James Corner Field Operations
logoResearch.verifiedFact: James Corner Field Operations is a New York landscape studio that designed the High Line with Diller Scofidio + Renfro.
observations: The short name fieldoperations runs together as one heavy lowercase word.
The founder's name is dropped from the logo, leaving the work to speak.

logoResearch.name: West 8
logoResearch.verifiedFact: West 8 is a landscape and urban design studio founded in Rotterdam in 1987 by Adriaan Geuze.
observations: Extended heavy capitals make the short name wide and bold.
The number 8 is drawn as part of the type, not as a symbol.

logoResearch.name: Gustafson Porter + Bowman
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Gustafson Porter + Bowman is a London landscape studio that designed the Diana, Princess of Wales Memorial Fountain.
observations: The three names are stacked in a thin grey sans, like labels on a plan.
A plus sign adds the third partner, just like DS+R.

logoResearch.name: Kelly Wearstler
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kelly Wearstler is a Los Angeles interior designer known for bold hotels and homes.
observations: Extended heavy capitals give the designer's name a fashion-label feel.
The name is the brand, like a couture house.

logoResearch.name: Neri&Hu
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Neri&Hu was founded in Shanghai in 2004 by Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu.
observations: An ampersand ties the two lowercase surnames together without spaces.
A thin sans keeps the logo light and modern.

logoResearch.name: SWA Group
logoResearch.verifiedFact: SWA Group is a landscape architecture firm founded in 1957 as Sasaki, Walker and Associates.
observations: Three heavy lowercase letters are rounded and friendly.
The initials keep a long founding name short.

logoResearch.name: Sasaki
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sasaki was founded in 1953 by landscape architect Hideo Sasaki and works from Boston and Shanghai.
observations: Each letter is built from coloured blocks, like a map or a model.
The multicolour wordmark is the most playful logo in this list.

listIntro: The boards below show all 45 architecture firm logos in one consistent format, grouped into global firms, signature studios, international firms, design-led practices, and interior and landscape studios.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the firm's size or buildings.
sectionIntroductions: The largest architecture and engineering firms work on airports, hospitals, and towers worldwide, and their logos favour bold, reliable type that works on any project board.
Signature studios are known for their founders and their buildings, and their logos are short, confident, and often built from initials.
Firms from Japan, Hong Kong, Scandinavia, and Australia show how local design culture shapes a logo, from Japanese precision to Scandinavian simplicity.
These studios are smaller and more design-led, and their logos are more personal, from typewriter type to interlocking letters.
Interior designers and landscape architects work closer to fashion and nature, so their logos are softer, wider, and sometimes colourful.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of architecture firm logos, not a ranking of firms.
Look at how each logo uses type, spacing, and one idea to reflect how the studio designs buildings.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a drawing title block, a competition board, or a site hoarding.

findings.heading: Architecture logos are mostly type
findings.text: Almost every firm in this list uses a wordmark or initials. SOM, KPF, OMA, Arup, and RPBW show that well-chosen type is enough when the buildings do the talking.

findings.heading: Initials replace long partner names
findings.text: Firms named after several founders, like SOM, KPF, HOK, and MVRDV, shorten them to initials that work on drawings and signage.

findings.heading: The best logos borrow from the buildings
findings.text: ZHA cuts its letters like its angular forms, BIG spells its name with building shapes, and Kengo Kuma & Associates draws letters with thin lines like timber slats.

findings.heading: Colour is rare and deliberate
findings.text: Gensler red, the HOK red square, and the Sasaki multicolour letters stand out precisely because almost every other firm uses black.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for an architecture firm logo
checklistItems: Does the logo work in the title block of a drawing and on a competition board?
Is it typographic and precise, rather than a generic house or roof icon?
Does it reflect one idea from how the studio designs?
Does it frame your project photography instead of competing with it?
Will it still read when printed small, in one colour, and on a site hoarding?

faq.question: What makes a good architecture firm logo?
faq.answer: A good architecture firm logo is typographic, precise, and restrained. It works on drawings, competition boards, websites, and site hoardings, and it adds one idea that reflects how the studio designs, like the cut letters of ZHA or the building shapes in the BIG logo.

faq.question: Should an architecture firm logo use a house or building icon?
faq.answer: Usually not. Most leading firms, like SOM, Foster + Partners, and Snøhetta, avoid literal house or skyline icons because they look generic. A distinctive wordmark or monogram is more memorable and lets the firm's buildings speak for themselves.

faq.question: Why do so many architecture firms use initials?
faq.answer: Many firms are named after several founding partners, so names like Skidmore, Owings & Merrill or Kohn Pedersen Fox become SOM and KPF. Initials are shorter, easier to read on drawings, and work like a monogram.

faq.question: What colours do architecture firm logos use?
faq.answer: Most architecture firm logos are black, grey, or white so they frame the projects rather than compete with them. A few firms, like Gensler, HOK, and Sasaki, use one strong colour as their signature.
